frontmatter.title: Sensing Sound and Music
frontmatter.description: This page describes the motivation behind making a web resource for the course MUS2640 Sensing Sound and Music at the University of Oslo.

children.value: This textbook is written for the course
at the University of Oslo. The course is a foundation for later studies in
is produced in the world, captured and represented by devices, and experienced in body and mind.
Having completed the course, you will:
be familiar with principles of how musical sound is produced and perceived.
understand relationships between sound-theoretical and music-theoretical concepts.
be able to process, synthesise, and analyse sound.

The course is organised for 12 teaching weeks with 2–3 hours of in-class work per week. You should plan roughly 6 hours of reading and assignments outside class each week. The course schedule below maps each week to a chapter, core ideas, and suggested activities.

Sensing, sound, music; interdisciplinarity; the two frames of the course: four levels of description (air, file, ear, mind) and the musicking quadrant (creation and experience, in time and out of time)
Course goals, fields, disciplinarities; where a claim sits and who is engaged
in your own words; place one musical situation you know in the quadrant; try one app from the intro list
Soundscape, ways of describing sound, artistic and scientific approaches
Sound studies vs acoustics vs psychoacoustics
Two-minute closed-eyes listen; short sound journal
Waves, rooms, instruments: causes of what we hear
Sonic Visualiser plots on a sound you choose
Capture, conversion, digital audio, monitors: technology chain
Recording chain for one of your own setups; LittleBits synth-kit exploration
Ear, loudness, pitch, masking, illusions: from physics to perception
Demo predictions for masking / continuity illusion
Spectral and symbolic views; expectation and structure
Embodiment; movement, motion, action and gesture; motion capture and video analysis
Performer and perceiver; embodied cognition; what a sensor measures against what a person infers
Record or describe body motion while listening or performing
Autonomic responses; HR, HRV, EDA, breathing
Relate one physiological idea to your own listening
Auditory–visual integration, the eye and its motion, eye tracking and pupillometry, gaze in performance
Auditory–visual against audio–video, and why audiovisual is avoided; McGurk and the binding window; the three confounds of the pupil
Note where you look against what you hear; try the eye tracker app
Regions and pathways; memory, attention, expectation; reward and chills; EEG, MEG, fMRI and fNIRS; brain–computer interfaces and music therapy
Methods trade-offs; consumer against research EEG
Live EEG with the Muse headbands: eyes closed and alpha, artefacts, an evoked response; identify claim, evidence, method and limits in one study
Audio features, MIR, AI, ethics; what a machine listener borrows from every earlier chapter
Run or inspect one feature plot; name the chapter each stage draws on
Alongside the twelve chapters there is a thirteenth page,

, which is not tied to any week. It collects the practical craft the course assumes but does not teach in class, in four parts: reading a research article and reading it critically; writing, from the question to the reference list, with the words that trip people up; reading and making spectrograms; and studying for the exam. It is meant to be consulted when you are planning a text or revising, rather than read straight through.
You can also check out the
, which is a compilation of terms with descriptions.
Students in this course have mixed backgrounds. Most have some musical experience, from classical performance to studio production, and non-performing music-lovers are equally welcome.
Some students come from musicology, others from psychology, informatics, media studies, philosophy, linguistics, medicine, and more. This mix is what makes the
discussions in class possible. The in-class activities are adjusted to the knowledge and experience of the group.

. Instead of sitting through lectures and taking notes, you work with the material: you discuss it, ask questions, try things out, and respond to each other’s work. Much of the class time is spent on group discussions, hands-on experiments, peer review, and small projects.
approach. It requires that you read, watch, and listen on your own. Then we can spend class time for discussing it and do hands-on activities.

course. The content builds on current research, and the teachers are all active researchers who bring in perspectives from their own projects. Much of this work follows scientific methods, but because of the subject matter we also draw on design-centred and artistic research. We will return to these differences along the way, since the
question of how each tradition justifies what it claims to know is itself worth understanding.
. You will take part in some ongoing research activities. This lets you see how research is done in practice, and it feeds back into ongoing projects at the
. You are welcome, though not required, to join in, for example, by contributing own data or taking part in one of our ongoing studies.
This course aims at merging theories and methods from
(and others). These are fields with different research traditions. When you read a paper or a summary, it can help to use a simple checklist for yourself:
: What is the main point of this study?

: What data or materials support it (listeners, musicians, audio examples, corpora, brain measures, motion capture, questionnaires)? What was found, in which direction and how large? The results are what the authors measured, not the earlier studies they review in the introduction.
: How were participants or materials chosen? What was measured or analysed? What baseline or control was used?

show (culture-specific listeners, short stimuli, lab vs concert, correlational vs causal)? What would falsify or qualify the claim? A statistical result supports or weakens a claim; it does not prove it.

These habits align with the course’s mix of quantitative experiments, qualitative inquiry, critical scholarship, and practice-based research. When it is your turn to write up what you have read, the reading and writing parts of
pick up where this checklist leaves off.
You may come across research with lots of statistics. Do not despair, you are not expected to understand this. However, whenever you come across something that is argued to be “
”, you should always question whether effect size and context are discussed, since statistical significance alone does not tell you whether something matters musically in everyday listening.
The course material follows the idea of
. Everything here is freely and openly available, during the course and afterwards. Open material is easier to share, revisit, and build on, both inside the university and beyond it.
and its emphasis on transparency, accessibility, and reproducibility. In this course we try to follow those principles by sharing:
: Most of the required reading is openly available, either genuinely free (“free as in speech”) or through the university’s institutional agreements (“free as in beer”).
: Where we can, the datasets used in the course are shared openly, so you can analyse, visualise, and interpret them yourself.
: The tools, scripts, and examples are shared as open-source code that you can read, modify, and reuse.
Working this way also makes it easier for you to contribute back rather than only consume.
In this course we actively explore
(AI). Many AI tools exist, but few are well understood in teaching. We will try several and judge for ourselves how well they work.
This textbook is itself an example of AI-assisted

. It has been written with the support of various large language models (LLMs). However, every part has been read and corrected by a human. During the course we will look at where AI writing can be trusted and where it breaks down.

You are encouraged to use AI for learning, but to use it wisely. It can explain a concept or give you quick feedback, but it is there to support your thinking, not to replace it. The exam is done without any tools, so in the end you have to be able to think and write on your own.
Check out the resources available at
for overviews of available tools and guidelines for usage.
We will try out a range of tools during the semester. The aim is not to master any single one, but to see how each works and what it is suited for.

A set of small, interactive WebAudio apps written for this book. They run in a browser, on phones and laptops alike, and need no installation. Camera and audio analysis happens in the browser; recordings are not uploaded. The Hand synth downloads the MediaPipe runtime and model when it starts. The apps are linked from the relevant chapters and collected here for easy access.
: Build timbres by mixing eight harmonics over a variable fundamental, with instrument presets and a missing-fundamental toggle.
: Strike bell-, gong-, and marimba-like sounds built from partials at non-integer frequency ratios.
: Hear the noise colours (white, pink, brownian, blue, grey) as continuous textures or short impulses.
: Two sine tones with adjustable frequencies, showing each tone and the beating pattern of their sum.
: Draw on an empty spectrogram and hear the drawing turned into sound by an inverse FFT.
: Test how FFT window size trades time detail against frequency detail on clicks, close tones, and a chirp.
: Constructive and destructive interference, from cancelling sine tones to audible comb filtering on a music loop.
: Enter a room’s dimensions, see its first axial modes, and listen for the boom.
: A scrolling spectrogram of your microphone, analysed locally and never recorded.
: A small subtractive synthesiser with oscillator, filter, ADSR envelope, and keyboard.
: Degrade a music loop live by lowering the sample rate and bit depth.
: Sweep from 20 Hz to 20 kHz and play a pitch-discrimination game (not a medical test).
: Move a source around the head and hear the localisation cues separately or together (headphones required).
: Hear one three-source scene as a mono sum, a panned stereo mix, and an HRTF binaural rendering (headphones required).
: Endlessly rising or falling tones, stepped or as a Risset glissando.
: Compare just intonation with equal temperament and rank intervals by consonance.
: Build scales and modes on a pitch-class circle and keyboard, in equal temperament or just intonation.
: Build chords and play progressions and cadences with voice leading and a live key estimate.
: Draw a melody, see its contour and intervals, and test your expectations against a folksong model.
: The alternating-tone experiment: find where one stream becomes two.
: Repeat a click at 1 to 1000 per second and hear separate pulses fuse into a tone.
: Group a cycle of pulses into equal or unequal beats, from 2/4 to 11/8 and beyond, drawn as a circle and a line.
: Drag every onset of a groove early or late and hear the difference between the grid and the shifted version.
: Draw a bar of kick, snare, and hi-hats on an eighth, triplet, or sixteenth grid and hear how subdivision changes the feel.
: Silence clicks and events in a looping bar, drop the pulse for whole bars, and rotate a rhythm against the beat.
: Tap for 20 s without feedback and get your spontaneous motor tempo, or watch your intervals live.
: Tap along with a click and see your timing accuracy, with an adjustable swing ratio.
: A paced-breathing guide and pulse-counting timer, no sensors needed.
: Heart rate from a fingertip over the phone camera or from the face in a webcam.
: The breathing waveform and rate from a phone on the chest or from a webcam.
: How a video eye tracker works: pupil detection, calibration, scanpaths, and pupil size, from a webcam.
: Live webcam motion images, quantity of motion, videograms, motiongrams, and a self-similarity matrix.
: A video’s motiongram and spectrogram on one timeline, from a file or a clip recorded with the camera.
: Turn webcam motion into sound, with the motiongram played as a spectrum.
: Use a MediaPipe hand tracker to control tone loudness with a right-hand pinch and pitch with the distance between both index knuckles.
We will use the following software, most of which are free and/or open source. They are also cross-platform, meaning they work on Windows, macOS, and Linux.
: A tool for viewing and analysing the contents of audio files. It allows you to visualise waveforms and spectrograms and to extract audio features.
: A widely used tool for recording, editing, and processing audio files, making it versatile for both beginners and advanced users in music and sound analysis.
: An open-source web application that enables you to create and share documents containing live code, equations, visualisations, and narrative text.
: A visual programming language widely used for sound synthesis, audio processing, and interactive installations. It resembles the commercial software
: A tool for exploring and organising sound samples through a visual interface. It helps you discover relationships between sounds and create new compositions.
: A collaborative online database of sound samples. It provides access to a wide range of sounds for music production, sound design, and research.
: An experimental web-based tool for studying musical rhythms, including the ability to record tapping patterns for research applications.
We will use these free, cross-platform apps on both Android and iOS devices.
: A mobile app for recording, analysing, and reporting environmental noise.
: A mobile app for recording and visualising sensor data from your smartphone, such as accelerometer, gyroscope, magnetometer, and more.
We will explore these devices in class. You are not expected to purchase these yourself; they are available to borrow.
: A platform of modular electronic components that snap together to create interactive projects. It is a hands-on way to explore sound synthesis and music-making.
: A portable recorder designed for capturing 360-degree spatial audio. It is ideal for creating immersive soundscapes and exploring 3D audio reproduction.
: A high-precision, infrared, camera-based motion capture system used for tracking motion in 3D space.
: Wearable devices designed to monitor physiological data such as heart rate, respiration, and body temperature.
: Portable eye trackers that can be used for tracking where one looks while also capturing gaze and pupil size.
The current textbook comprises the core curriculum for this course. Interested readers can find more information in the texts listed below, as well as in the references section for each chapter.
Music Psychology: A Very Short Introduction
: An introduction to the field of music psychology, exploring how music affects the mind and behaviour.
Music and Technology: A Very Short Introduction
: An overview of the relationship between music and technology, examining its impact on creation, performance, and listening.
Ways of Listening: An Ecological Approach to the Perception of Musical Meaning
: An introduction to how listeners perceive and interpret musical meaning in ecological contexts.
: An examination of musical instruments as tools for interaction, creativity, and expression.
Some books are large-scale references for their fields:
: A reference for experimental and empirical approaches to the study of music.
Music and Science: A Guide to Empirical Music Research
: An overview of scientific approaches to music psychology research.
The Oxford Handbook of Music Psychology
: A comprehensive overview of research and theories in music psychology.
The Computer Music Tutorial, Second Edition
(2023), Cambridge: The MIT Press. A large volume covering all aspects of computer music, from sound synthesis to interaction.
There are not many relevant books in Norwegian, but here are some:
(2005), Oslo: Universitetsforlaget. An introductory Norwegian textbook covering key perspectives and approaches in musicology.
(2009), Oslo: Unipub. A Norwegian book exploring the relationship between music and body movement.
Lydlandskap: Om Bruk og Misbruk av Musikk
(2005), Bergen: Fagbokforlaget. A Norwegian book discussing the use and misuse of music in various contexts.

This course covers the psychological aspects of music perception and cognition, including auditory perception, emotional responses to music, and the cognitive processes involved in listening, performing, and composing.

This course covers the meeting point of music and technology: sound synthesis, digital audio processing, and algorithmic composition, with hands-on work using tools for creating and analysing music computationally.
